title: The Algerian War
subject: histoire
description: For **eight years**, France fought a war of independence on land it insisted was its own. The Algerian War brought down the Fourth Republic and left lasting scars.

hero.hook: Eight years of war that France long refused to call a war.

blocks.text: The Algerian War (**1954-1962**) is one of the most painful chapters in 20th century French history. It was not simply a decolonization. For Paris, Algeria was not a distant colony: it was a piece of France itself.

For eight years the French state fought the **FLN**, the National Liberation Front, which demanded independence. The crisis brought down the Fourth Republic and gave birth to the Fifth. Long called “the events” or “law and order operations,” this war left torn memories on both shores of the Mediterranean.

Conquered from **1830** onward, Algeria was carved up as early as **1848** into [[French departments]]. For many people, leaving Algeria meant cutting away part of the nation itself. In **1954** it held about **9 million** Muslims and **1 million** Europeans, the [[Pieds-noirs]].
Until **1999**, French law refused the word “war.” The official term was “law and order operations,” which kept FLN fighters from being treated as prisoners of war.

blocks.caption: FLN fighters during the Algerian War

blocks.text: On **May 8, 1945**, while Europe celebrated victory, the army crushed demonstrations at Sétif and Guelma in eastern Algeria, killing thousands. On **November 1, 1954**, came the “Red All Saints' Day”: the FLN set off some sixty attacks. **François Mitterrand**, then interior minister, summed up the official line: “Algeria is France.”

In 1956, Parliament voted the [[special powers]] law and handed the army full police authority. Nearly **400,000** soldiers, many of them conscripts, fanned out across the country against FLN [[guerrilla warfare]], a war of ambushes and bombings.

blocks.caption: Algiers, 1957: urban war in the heart of the capital

blocks.text: In **1957**, during the **Battle of Algiers**, paratroopers under General **Jacques Massu** broke up the bomb networks. It was a military victory and a moral defeat: torture became a routine way to get information. In mainland France the scandal grew. The country tore itself apart over whether its own war was legitimate.

sections.title: De Gaulle and the turning point

blocks.text: On **May 13, 1958**, Algiers rose up to keep “French Algeria.” **Charles de Gaulle** returned to power and founded the Fifth Republic. Seen at first as the savior of French sovereignty, he quickly understood that holding on was impossible. He steered the country toward self-determination: letting Algerians choose their own future.

blocks.caption: De Gaulle facing the Algerian question

blocks.text: In April **1961**, the [[Generals' putsch]] in Algiers tried to topple him. After it failed, the [[OAS]], the Secret Army Organization, stepped up its bombings to block any negotiation.

The **Évian Accords** of **March 18, 1962** set the [[ceasefire]]. On July 1, a referendum approved independence. The violence did not stop. The [[harkis]], Muslim soldiers who had fought alongside France, were abandoned and killed by the thousands. Nearly a million Pieds-noirs fled to mainland France.

blocks.text: The Algerian War (**1954-1962**) ended the French colonial empire. It left a painful legacy: torture, the exodus of the Pieds-noirs, and the abandonment of the harkis.
